تطالب إسرائيل بالإفراج عن 350 طفلاً فلسطينياً وإنهاء اعتقالهم دون محاكمة ❚❚ السبت، 21 نوفمبر 2026 حمّل التطبيق آيفون حمّل التطبيق أندرويد الجريدة PDF أرسل مقالك البحث بحث ☰ الأقسام الصفحة الرئيسية مصر الأزمة الإنسانية في السودان تحرير أخبار الغد وقت النشر: 9:31 م 20 نوفمبر، 2026 شارك: واتساب فيسبوك إكس تيليجرام إنستجرام وتطبيقات أخرى نسخ الرابط أدوات القراءة طباعة أ + أ − تصاعدت هجمات المسيّرات في السودان، ما أدى إلى تفاقم الأزمة الإنسانية، الأمر الذي بحثه مجلس الأمن الدولي خلال جلسة مغلقة عُقدت اليوم الجمعة، وسط تحذيرات من التدهور المستمر للأوضاع وازدياد خطر المجاعة. وعقد أعضاء مجلس الأمن الدولي جلسة لبحث تطورات الأوضاع الإنسانية والانفلات الأمني في السودان، بدعوة من الدانمارك وبريطانيا، قبيل مفاوضات مرتقبة حول نظام العقوبات على البلاد. واستمع المجلس إلى إحاطة من الأمين العام المساعد للشؤون الإنسانية محمد يحيى، الذي وصف الوضع في السودان بأنه «كارثي»، مشيرًا إلى النزاع والنزوح والجفاف ونقص التمويل كأسباب رئيسية لأزمة الغذاء المتفاقمة. أخبار متعلقة السودان على حافة الهاوية: الجفاف والصراع يهددان الملايين بالمجاعة الطريق الضيق باليمن: مجلس الأمن يقرع ناقوس الخطر للملاحة تصعيد أفريقي: شبكة النساء السودانيات تطالب الاتحاد بسحب ترحيبه بالحوار وأظهرت بيانات «التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي» خطر المجاعة المتزايد في بعض مناطق دارفور وكردفان نتيجة الأعمال العدائية والنزوح الجماعي والجفاف الشديد وضعف التمويل الإنساني. وأشار يحيى إلى أن العمليات الإنسانية تواجه قيودًا وصعوبات شديدة، خاصة في ظل ظاهرة «النينيو» وتحديات وصول المساعدات للمناطق الأكثر تضررًا. وكانت منسقة الأمم المتحدة في السودان دينيس براون قد حذرت من تعطل مئات الشاحنات الإنسانية بسبب نقص الوقود، وذكرت أن المستشفيات تكافح للاستمرار مع تراجع تمويل برامج الإغاثة. ووفق تقرير لمكتب المفوض السامي للأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان، فإن الاستخدام المتزايد للطائرات المسيّرة من أطراف النزاع تسبب في مقتل أكثر من 1600 مدني من إجمالي 2230 حالة وفاة موثقة منذ بداية العام وحتى أكتوبر الماضي، واستهدف الهجمات بنى تحتية حيوية في 11 ولاية، مما أدى إلى انقطاع الكهرباء وتعطيل الخدمات الأساسية. وأدانت اللجنة الخماسية الدولية، التي تضم الاتحاد الأفريقي و«إيغاد» وجامعة الدول العربية والاتحاد الأوروبي والأمم المتحدة، تصعيد استخدام المسيّرات محذرةً من تداعياتها على المدنيين والعمليات الإنسانية. في الوقت نفسه، لا تزال الجهود الدولية متعثرة لتحقيق هدنة أو إطلاق عملية سياسية شاملة، رغم التحركات المستمرة من قبل مبعوث الأمم المتحدة والمجموعة الرباعية الإقليمية. وتأتي هذه التطورات في ظل استعداد مجلس الأمن لمناقشة مستقبل نظام العقوبات المفروض على السودان، حيث تقترح الولايات المتحدة توسيع حظر الأسلحة ليشمل السودان بالكامل ويغطي الطائرات المسيّرة، لكن الاقتراح يواجه معارضة من عدة دول تفضل الإبقاء على النطاق الجغرافي الحالي للعقوبات. يذكر أن نظام العقوبات الدولي على السودان المُمدد حتى 11 ديسمبر المقبل يخضع لمراجعة دورية، في وقت تتفاقم فيه المعاناة الإنسانية وتتصاعد المطالب بضغط دولي لوقف التصعيد وتحسين الوضع sudan.summary: عقد مجلس الأمن الدولي جلسة مغلقة لمناقشة تصاعد هجمات المسيّرات في السودان وتأثيرها على الأزمة الإنسانية المتفاقمة. وقد دعا كل من الدانمارك وبريطانيا إلى الاجتماع، حيث تم استعراض الوضع الكارثي في البلاد من قبل الأمين العام المساعد للشؤون الإنسانية، محمد يحيى. وأشار يحيى إلى أن النزاع والجفاف ونقص التمويل يساهمون في تفاقم أزمة الغذاء، مع تزايد خطر المجاعة في مناطق مثل دارفور وكردفان. كما أظهرت التقارير أن استخدام المسيّرات أدى إلى مقتل أكثر من 1600 مدني منذ بداية العام. في ظل هذه الظروف، تواجه العمليات الإنسانية صعوبات كبيرة، بما في ذلك نقص الوقود الذي يعطل شحنات المساعدات. بينما تسعى الولايات المتحدة لتوسيع حظر الأسلحة ليشمل المسيّرات، تواجه هذه الاقتراحات معارضة من بعض الدول. يتزامن ذلك مع استمرار الجهود الدولية لتحقيق هدنة سياسية في السودان.

sudan.title: السودان يندد بالهجمات على السعودية والكويت - سودان تربيون
sudan.content: السودان يندد بالهجمات على السعودية والكويت - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 21 نوفمبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر السودان يندد بالهجمات على السعودية والكويت اختيار المحرر السودان يندد بالهجمات على السعودية والكويت 20 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الدول العربية , السودان 0 المقر السابق لوزارة الخارجية في الخرطوم الخرطوم 20 نوفمبر 2026 – نددت الحكومة السودانية، الجمعة، بالهجمات التي استهدفت منشآت مدنية في السعودية والكويت، حيث تتصاعد الهجمات الصاروخية وهجمات الطائرات المسيّرة على منشآت مدنية في هذه الدول. وتتعرض مواقع في عدد من دول الخليج، منذ أشهر، لهجمات بالصواريخ الباليستية والطائرات المسيّرة القادمة من إيران، وذلك على خلفية التصعيد العسكري والغارات الجوية التي تشنها الولايات المتحدة الأميركية على الأراضي الإيرانية بين الحين والآخر. كما تعرضت المملكة العربية السعودية، خلال الفترة الماضية، لهجمات بصواريخ باليستية وطائرات مسيّرة أطلقتها جماعة الحوثيين في اليمن، على خلفية النزاع اليمني والتدخل العسكري للتحالف العربي لدعم الشرعية بقيادة المملكة ضد الجماعة المدعومة من إيران. وقالت وزارة الخارجية، في بيان، إنها “تعرب عن كامل تضامنها مع دولة الكويت الشقيقة، وتدين الاعتداءات التي استهدفت أراضيها باستخدام الطائرات المسيّرة، في انتهاك سافر لسيادتها وتهديد لأمنها واستقرارها”. وأعلنت رفض السودان كافة الاعتداءات التي تستهدف سيادة الدول وسلامة أراضيها، وشددت على أن أمن دولة الكويت وسلامة مواطنيها جزء لا يتجزأ من أمن واستقرار المنطقة. وجددت الحكومة السودانية وقوفها التام إلى جانب دولة الكويت، وتأييدها لكل ما تتخذه من إجراءات مشروعة لحماية أمنها وسيادتها وصون سلامة أراضيها، داعيةً إلى وقف التصعيد وتغليب لغة الحوار والحلول الدبلوماسية، بما يحفظ أمن المنطقة واستقرارها. وفي بيان ثانٍ، أعلنت الخارجية السودانية عن إدانة الحكومة واستنكارها الشديدين للاعتداءات التي استهدفت منشآت مدنية واقتصادية في العاصمة السعودية الرياض، وما أسفرت عنه من أضرار الصورة من صفحة الشركة السودانية لتوزيع الغاز على الفيس بوك نهر النيل – الشمالية: 20 نوفمبر 2026- راديو دبنقا ​شهدت الولاية الشمالية ارتفاعاً جديداً في أسعار غاز الطهي ليصل سعر تعبئة الأسطوانة إلى مستويات قياسية تراوحت بين 228 ألف و230 ألف جنيه، وسط شح في المعروض وتباين في توفر الإمدادات وفق إفادات مواطنين ومصادر ميدانية في عدد من المدن من بينها دنقلا ومروي. ​وتأتي هذه الزيادة في وقت تشهد فيه حركة التوزيع والتسعير في الولاية الشمالية تجاذبات بين السلطات المحلية ووكلاء الغاز بشأن كلفة الترحيل وتحديد الأسعار، حيث اعتمدت محلية دنقلا تسعيرة المستودع للأسطوانة زنة 12.5 كيلوغرام عند 218,602 جنيه استناداً إلى خطاب إدارة النقل العام والبترول بالولاية بشأن الشحنات الواردة من بورتسودان، بينما برزت خلافات مع وكلاء حول هوامش الترحيل والتوزيع. ​وفي سياق متصل أقرت وزارة المالية وإدارة النقل العام والبترول بولاية نهر النيل تعديلاً جديداً لأسعار أسطوانات غاز الطهي زنة 12.5 كيلوغرام اعتباراً من الخميس 19 نوفمبر 2026، حيث بلغ سعر البيع للمستهلك في محلية البحيرة 222 ألفاً و500 جنيه، مقابل 216 ألفاً و500 جنيه في الدامر وعطبرة، مع تحديد سعر الأسطوانة للوكيل الموزع في البحيرة عند 202 ألف و500 جنيه، وإقرار غرامات مالية مشددة على المخالفين للتسعيرة المعلنة. ​وتنعكس هذه القفزات السعرية بصورة مباشرة على الأسر والمخابز والأنشطة الخدمية في ظل تزايد أعباء المعيشة، ما يدفع مواطنين في عدد من المناطق إلى البحث عن بدائل تقليدية للطهي وسط مطالبات بضبط الإمدادات ومراجعة التسعير عند المصدر. انزلاق السودان نحو مجاعة وشيكة تهدد حياة الملايين، مطالبةً بوقف فوري للحرب وتأمين الممرات الإنسانية وإنقاذ الموسم الزراعي الشتوي. وأوضحت في بيان اطّلع عليه «راديو دبنقا»أن البلاد تشهد انهياراً شاملاً لمقومات الحياة وسبل كسب العيش وليس مجرد نقص عابر في الغذاء؛ وذلك جراء استمرار العمليات العسكرية، وتدمير الأسواق والبنية التحتية، وتعطيل سلاسل الإمداد، بالتزامن مع تعثر الموسم الزراعي وارتفاع أسعار المواد الغذائية إلى مستويات تفوق قدرة غالبية الأسر. وأشار البيان إلى أن النساء والفتيات والأطفال وكبار السن والأشخاص ذوي الإعاقة يتحملون العبء الأكبر من الكارثة، حيث تواجه النساء تحديات مضاعفة لتوفير الغذاء لأسرهن وسط انعدام مصادر الدخل وتزايد أعباء الرعاية، مما يعرضهن لمخاطر سوء التغذية والعنف والاستغلال. وحمّلت «منسم» طرفي النزاع وسلطات الأمر الواقع مسؤولية تعميق الأزمة وتدمير الاقتصاد الوطني، مشددةً على أن «الحق في الغذاء حق أصيل من حقوق الإنسان وليس منحة، ولا يجوز استخدامه كسلاح في الحرب أو وسيلة للعقاب الجماعي والابتزاز السياسي والعسكري». خارطة طريق وطرحت المجموعات النسوية خارطة طريق للإنقاذ تضمنت ثمانية محاور رئيسية، في مقدمتها مطالبة طرفي النزاع بالوقف الفوري وغير المشروط لإطلاق النار والانخراط في مسار سلمي يضع حماية المدنيين فوق أي اعتبارات عسكرية، إلى جانب فتح الطرق وتأمين الممرات الإنسانية لضمان وصول الغذاء والدواء والمياه دون عوائق أو تسييس مع إعطاء الأولوية للفئات الأكثر هشاشة. كما شددت الخارطة على ضرورة إنقاذ الموسم الزراعي الشتوي عبر توفير التمويل والبذور والأسمدة والوقود لصغار المنتجين والتعاونيات وحماية الأراضي الزراعية ومصادر المياه لتقليل الاعتماد على المساعدات الطارئة، بالتوازي مع دعم مبادرات الزراعة المنزلية للنساء في المدن والأرياف ومناطق النزوح وتزويدهن بالمدخلات والتمويل الصغير والإرشاد الفني. ودعت «منسم» كذلك إلى إطلاق حملة نسوية وطنية ودولية للمناصرة باللغات المختلفة للضغط من أجل وقف الحرب، وتوثيق شهادات النساء المتضررات من الجوع في وسائل الإعلام مع ضمان سلامتهن وحماية هويتهن، فضلاً عن تنظيم حوار نسوي موسع عبر منصة «زووم» بمشاركة خبيرات ومزارعات لمناقشة جذور الأزمة وصياغة أجندة نسوية للأمن الغذائي، ومطالبة الوكالات الأممية والمانحين باعتماد بيانات مصنفة حسب النوع الاجتماعي والعمر والإعاقة وإشراك المنظمات النسوية والقاعدية كشريكات في تصميم الاستجابة ومراقبتها. واكدت المجموعات على أن المساعدات الطارئة وحدها لن تعالج جذور الأزمة ما لم تتوقف الحرب وتُستعاد مصادر الإنتاج، مشددةً على أن «النساء لسن مجرد ضحايا أو متلقيات للمساعدات، بل فاعلات أساسيات في حماية الأمن الغذائي وصناعة الحلول، ولا يمكن بناء سلام مستدام دون ضمان مشاركتهن في القرار والموارد». 2026- مبادرة المجتمع المدني في النيل الأزرق النيل الأزرق- 20 نوفمبر 2026- راديو دبنقا أعلنت قوات تحالف السودان التأسيسي “تأسيس” عن تمكّن قواتها، اليوم الجمعة، من السيطرة 5 مناطق بإقليم النيل الأزرق – الفونج الجديد (خور ماك، المدينة 10، المدينة 11، سنجة نبق، وقرية الطاقة). وقال التحالف في بيان اطلع عليه “راديو دبنقا” أن قواتهم استولت على 27 عربة و6 دبابات ومدرعتين، فيما تم تدمير وحرق أكثر من 70 عربة تتبع للقوات المسلحة ومقتل المئات من الجنود. وأكدت أنها ستواصل القتال متعهدة بالعمل على ضمان حماية المدنيين، وتأمين الأسواق والمرافق العامة، وإعادة فتح الأسواق والخدمات الأساسية للمواطنين في جميع المناطق التي تمت السيطرة عليها. وكانت قوات تأسيس قد أعلنت أمس الخميس سيطرتها على مدينة باو ومنطقتي المدينة 12 وديرنق في محافظتي قيسان والكرمك بينما نفى محافظ باو ذلك. وبسيطرتها على منطقة باو تكون قوات تأسيس قد سيطرت على ثلاث من عواصم محافظات الإقليم ، وتكمن أهمية منطقة باو قربها من الدمازين حاضرة الإقليم حيث تبعد عنها 60 كيلومترا ويربطها بالمدينة طريق مسفلت. مبادرة مدنية تحذر حذرت مبادرة المجتمع المدني بإقليم النيل الأزرق من التطورات العسكرية المتسارعة في الإقليم، مع اتساع رقعة المواجهات واقتراب العمليات القتالية من عاصمة الإقليم، الدمازين، وما يترتب على ذلك من مخاطر جسيمة تهدد حياة المدنيين وتفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية والأمنية. وناشد الأمين العام للمبادرة علي هجو في حديثه لـ”راديو دبنقا” أطراف الحرب بالتحلي بالمسؤولية الأخلاقية والإنسانية تجاه المدنيين في المناطق التي تشهد عمليات عسكرية وفي كل يوم تتسع فيه رقعة الاشتباكات. مشيراً إلى أن المعارك امتدت منذ صباح اليوم إلى المنطقة 12 إلى 11 إلى 10 لمحافظة قيسان، وأن الاشتباكات مستمرة في القرى والمدن السكنية بالإضافة إلى محافظة باو ومناطق sudan.summary: أعلن تحالف السودان التأسيسي "تأسيس" عن سيطرته على خمس مناطق جديدة في إقليم النيل الأزرق، وهي الفونج الجديد، خور ماك، المدينة 10، المدينة 11، سنجة نبق، وقرية الطاقة. جاء ذلك في بيان نشرته قوات التحالف، حيث أكدت استيلاءها على 27 عربة و6 دبابات ومدرعتين، وتدمير أكثر من 70 عربة تابعة للقوات المسلحة، مما أسفر عن مقتل المئات من الجنود. كما تعهد التحالف بمواصلة القتال مع ضمان حماية المدنيين وإعادة فتح الأسواق والخدمات الأساسية. في المقابل، حذرت مبادرة المجتمع المدني في النيل الأزرق من تصاعد الأعمال العسكرية، مشيرة إلى المخاطر التي تهدد حياة المدنيين، خاصة مع اقتراب الاشتباكات من عاصمة الإقليم، الدمازين. وقد امتدت المعارك إلى مناطق جديدة، مما يزيد من تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية والأمنية في المنطقة.

sudan.content: «الدعم السريع» تعلن السيطرة على مناطق جديدة في النيل الأزرق - سودان تربيون الدعم السريع تعلن السيطرة على 5 مناطق بالنيل الأزرق تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 21 نوفمبر الازرق «الدعم السريع» تعلن السيطرة على مناطق جديدة في النيل الأزرق االنيل الازرق «الدعم السريع» تعلن السيطرة على مناطق جديدة في النيل الأزرق 20 نوفمبر 2026 في االنيل الازرق , اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , الحكومة الموازية , السودان , دول الجوار 0 قائد الحركة الشعبية بإقليم النيل الأزرق جوزيف توكا الدمازين 20 نوفمبر 2026 – قال تحالف قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية – شمال إن التحالف سيطر، الجمعة، على خمس مناطق جديدة في إقليم النيل الأزرق أقصى جنوب شرق السودان. ويأتي هذا التقدم بعد يوم من إعلان التحالف سيطرته على رئاسة محافظة باو، نحو 70 كيلومتراً جنوب غرب الدمازين عاصمة الإقليم، كثالث رئاسة محافظة يسيطر عليها التحالف بعد الكرمك وقيسان. وقال بيان لقوات الدعم السريع إن قوات «تأسيس» (قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية) سيطرت، اليوم الجمعة، على 5 مناطق بإقليم النيل الأزرق تشمل: خور ماك، والمدينة 10، والمدينة 11، وسنجة نبق، وقرية الطاقة، وهي مناطق تابعة لمحافظة قيسان وتقع على بعد حوالي 40 كيلومتراً جنوب شرق مدينة الدمازين. وأفاد البيان بأن قوات التحالف سيطرت على هذه المناطق وسط حالة من الانهيار في صفوف الجيش وأعوانه من المرتزقة، حسب تعبير البيان. وذكر البيان أن قوات التحالف قتلت وأسرت المئات من قوات العدو، فيما لاذ آخرون بالفرار، واستولت على 27 سيارة قتالية و6 دبابات ومدرعتين، كما دمرت وحرقت أكثر من 70 مركبة، وفقاً للبيان. وفي الأثناء، أبلغت مصادر محلية «سودان تربيون» بأن وصول المعارك إلى ديرنق وباو والقرى التي أعلنت قوات الدعم السريع السيطرة عليها تسبب في موجة نزوح جديدة إلى الدمازين، التي تستضيف عشرات الآلاف من النازحين في عدة مخيمات. ويُشار إلى أن جبهة القتال في إقليم النيل الأزرق أقصى جنوب شرق البلاد نشطت بين الجيش السوداني وتحالف قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية – شمال منذ يناير الماضي. وتمكن تحالف الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية من السيطرة على رئاسات محافظات الكُرمك وقِيسان وبَاو، فضلاً عن الاستيلاء على قواعد استراتيجية للجيش في بكوري بمحافظة قيسان وسركم وسالي بمحافظة الكرمك. الكلمات: الجيش السوداني الحرب في السودان الحركة الشعبية شمال الدعم السريع الدمازين النزوح النيل الأزرق باو قوات تأسيس قيسان. مقالات ذات صلة لحماية النساء والفتيات من الانتهاكات المتصاعدة جراء الحرب في السودان. وجاء النداء بمناسبة حملة الـ16 يوماً لمناهضة العنف ضد المرأة، تحت شعار “اتحدوا لإنهاء العنف ضد النساء والفتيات، وضمان العدالة، وحماية الناجيات، وإنهاء الإفلات من العقاب”. وأكد الملتقى، الذي يضم نساءً من خلفيات متنوعة، تشمل ناشطات المجتمع المدني وحقوق الإنسان، والأكاديميات والإعلاميات والقانونيات والنازحات واللاجئات والسياسيات ونساء الريف والرحّل، أن المناسبة لا ينبغي أن تقتصر على تجديد الالتزامات السنوية، بل يجب أن تتحول إلى خطوات عملية وعاجلة لحماية النساء والفتيات، وتعزيز آليات العدالة ومحاسبة مرتكبي الانتهاكات. وأوضح أن نساء دارفور دفعن الثمن الأكبر للنزاعات المسلحة منذ عام 2003، وأن معاناتهن تفاقمت بصورة غير مسبوقة منذ اندلاع الحرب في 15 أبريل 2023، في ظل استمرار أعمال العنف والنزوح القسري والانتهاكات الجسيمة بحق النساء والفتيات. وأشار النداء إلى تجدد مأساة النزوح في عدد من معسكرات دارفور، حيث اضطرت نساء كنّ طفلات يحملن على ظهور أمهاتهن خلال موجات النزوح السابقة، إلى الفرار مجدداً، وهن اليوم أمهات يحملن أطفالهن بحثاً عن الأمان. أوضاع مأساوية في الجنينة وسلط الملتقى الضوء على الأوضاع الإنسانية المأساوية في مدينة الجنينة بولاية غرب دارفور، مشيراً إلى تعرض النساء لأشكال متعددة من الانتهاكات، شملت القتل والتهجير والاغتصاب والاستغلال الجنسي وزواج الطفلات، في ظل تدهور الأوضاع المعيشية وانقطاع فرص التعليم. وفي مدينة الفاشر بولاية شمال دارفور، أشار الملتقى إلى تعرض النساء والفتيات لانتهاكات منسوبة إلى أطراف الصراع، شملت التهجير القسري والنزوح واللجوء والاستغلال الجنسي، فضلاً عن فقدان مصادر الدخل واضطرار بعض النساء إلى ممارسة أعمال هامشية تزيد من تعرضهن للاستغلال والمخاطر. أما مدينة طويلة بشمال دارفور، التي تستضيف أعداداً كبيرة من النازحين من مناطق دارفور وكردفان، فقد أكد الملتقى أن النساء يواجهن فيها تحديات إنسانية واجتماعية خطيرة، رغم الاستقرار الأمني النسبي، أبرزها الاستغلال الجنسي وانعدام سبل العيش الكريم وصعوبة الوصول إلى العدالة. وشدد الملتقى على أن استمرار هذه الانتهاكات يهدد مستقبل النساء والأطفال، ويضاعف من حجم الكارثة الإنسانية، مؤكداً ضرورة الاستجابة الدولية العاجلة استناداً إلى أحكام القانون الدولي الإنساني وقرار مجلس الأمن رقم 1325 بشأن المرأة والسلام والأمن. و طرح الملتقى 12 مطلباً عاجلاً أبرزها إلزام أطراف الصراع بالوقف الفوري لإطلاق النار، وحماية المدنيين من خلال إصدار قرار دولي بموجب الفصل السابع من ميثاق الأمم المتحدة، وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية عبر فتح ممرات آمنة. كما دعا إلى تعزيز شبكات حماية النساء، وإنشاء مدن ومساحات آمنة للنساء والأطفال، ودعم المنظمات النسوية العاملة على الأرض، وتوفير الدعم الفني واللوجستي للاجئات السودانيات في معسكرات شرق تشاد. وطالب المجتمع الدولي بدعم المؤسسات التعليمية والصحية، وتوسيع نطاق المساعدات الغذائية التي يقدمها برنامج الأغذية العالمي لتشمل جميع المناطق المتضررة في دارفور، مع إعطاء الأولوية للنساء والأطفال والنازحين واللاجئين. وشملت المطالب أيضاً توفير خدمات الدعم النفسي والاجتماعي والمساعدة القانونية للضحايا والناجين من الانتهاكات، إلى جانب تفعيل آليات المساءلة الدولية، وملاحقة جميع المتورطين في جرائم الحرب والجرائم ضد الإنسانية، وضمان عدم إفلاتهم من العقاب. وأعرب عن تقديره للجهود الدولية الرامية إلى إحلال السلام في السودان، داعياً إلى ترجمة هذه الجهود إلى إجراءات ملموسة تضع حماية المدنيين، ولا سيما النساء والفتيات، في مقدمة الأولويات. وقال الملتقى أن نساء دارفور لا يطلبن التعاطف وحده، وإنما يطالبن بالحماية والعدالة والإنصاف والحق في الحياة الكريمة والآمنة. وشدد أن “ان لا سلام دون عدالة، ولا عدالة دون محاسبة، ولا مستقبل للسودان إذا تركت النساء وحدهن يواجهن العنف”. ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa 20 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited African leaders, health experts, and global partners to Addis Ababa for the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), calling for collective action to build a healthier and more resilient continent. In a video message shared on social media, the Prime Minister announced that Ethiopia will host the conference from November 23 to 27 at the Addis International Convention Center. The event will be co-hosted by Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The conference is expected to bring together heads of state, ministers, researchers, innovators, and development partners to strengthen continental cooperation and advance African-led solutions to public health challenges, he said. PM Abiy said Ethiopia was proud to host the important gathering and looking forward to welcoming leaders, researchers, and partners from across Africa and beyond. The conference provides an important opportunity to unite knowledge, strengthen partnerships, and advance African-led solutions to the continent's health priorities, the Prime Minister underscored. "Together, let us turn shared aspirations into collective action and build a healthier, more resilient Africa," the Prime Minister underscored, adding, "Africa is ready." Held under the theme "Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty," CPHIA 2026 will focus on reducing external dependence in the health sector, strengthening resilient healthcare systems, and advancing African ownership of public health priorities. ethiopia.title: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Negasi Awetehey Addis Abeba — Tigray's dynamic relationship with the modern Ethiopian state has been shaped by a historical paradox and contradiction: Tigray has been both a target of state oppression, betrayal, and genocide and, at critical moments, an influential participant in shaping the Ethiopian state itself. The Meles Zenawi era brought a long-awaited sense of relief and ecstasy to the people of Tigray after years of struggle, suffering, and uncertainty. This shift from prolonged agony to renewed hope was captured in the title of the late Dr. Solomon Enkuay's book, The Agony and Ecstasy of Tigray --a title that evokes historical contradictions: the enduring pain of oppression and conflict, alongside the exhilaration of hard-won political transformation and a new social contract. Under the EPRDF-led Ethiopian state, the people of Tigray were encouraged to believe in a shared identity founded on self-determination, equality, and mutual respect. Placing uncritical faith in the Ethiopian state, Tigrayans prioritized peace, development, and coexistence, often at the expense of safeguarding Tigray's long-term benefits. Today, that trust has been shattered, leaving behind a profound sense of collective betrayal. The promise of equality, mutual respect, and unity in diversity has become an illusion. Hated throughout history, yet ever-present Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The land of Tigray has witnessed some of the most frequent and brutal battles in human history. Millennial before the formation of Ethiopia, Tigray endured wars. Before the 2020 war, I used to hear elders saying more than 30 battles had been fought in Tigray. Figures from the center to dehumanize, especially driven by the hate of the 1970s/80s TPLF movement in the north but Tigrayans, manipulate and label it ' ሰሜኑ ሁሌ ጦርነት: የተረገመ ምድር' (the north is always at war: the cursed land). From an archaeological perspective, the earliest destruction dates back to the D'mt period (5th century BC). This was destruction of monumental temples and palaces an era when there was no world order, security and sovereignty, when a powerful empire from afar could invade any group or polity at will. Tigray, even in the age of world order and sovereignty, has endured foreign invasions and wars. Ethiopia's political sovereignty has done little to ensure the security and sovereignty of the Tigray people. Leaving ancient conflicts aside, modern wars in Tigray have put the state acting as either an indifferent or an aggressor or in alliance with the foreign forces. There was also a process that, under the guise of nation-building, the Ethiopian state fractured Tigray's territory and stripped its autonomy and capacity--deliberately leaving it weak and vulnerable to foreign invasion and internal suppression. Because the agency is in the hands of the Ethiopian state, and the same agency adding other foreign agencies has been used to invade Tigray. The 2020-2022 war waged against Tigray by the Prosperity Party-led Ethiopia demonstrates that one hardly needs to study history to witness this ugliest repetition. This government's attempt to decimate Tigray brought Eritrean forces and other drone powers with geopolitical interests. History repeats itself, but each repetition grows uglier. Another unsettling pattern for Tigray is that the broader Ethiopian populace within the country's map is not aware of Ethiopia's sovereignty and the dignity of its people. Instead, they have been manipulated into aligning with foreign forces to annihilate their own fraternal neighbor, Tigray. Meresa Tsehaye, a scholar of political science and security studies, underscores Tigray's dual position as a historically marginalized periphery within the modern Ethiopian state and a strategic part of the wider Horn of Africa. Caught between regional rivalries and competing geopolitical interests, Tigray remains vulnerable to the ambitions of global powers, Middle Eastern actors, and East African states. These overlapping geopolitical, geo-cultural, and geostrategic dynamics risk perpetuating Tigray's role as a hotspot of regional instability, where external interests overshadow its people's rights, security, and aspirations. The recurring cycle of invasion underscores the imperative of a sovereign future for Tigray. The only way to prevent war--the ugliest reality Tigrayans have abhorred throughout history, yet one that remains ever-present--is to secure the future and sovereignty. The Ethiopian government's war on Tigray started in 2020 but has never stopped. The exercise of Tigray's right to self-determination has been pushed aside. Unless this trajectory is reversed, Tigray faces the risk of being erased from the map and its people being wiped out. If this is not possible, political subjugation and assimilation remain the likely scenarios. Reversing this course is imperative for Tigray to safeguard its people, restore their dignity, and secure their right to determine their own future. Existential incompatibility of PP Ideology, Tigray nationalism The relationship between the PP's ideology and Tigrayan identity is fundamentally defined by a profound asymmetry: that between the perpetrator and the victim of betrayal, genocide, and violence. Their relationship is characterized by a fundamental contradiction--one resembling that between the killer and the killed, the perpetrator and the victim, or the betrayer and the betrayed. Although the word "Prosperity" ostensibly evokes progress, growth, and development, it has acquired an altogether different and deeply pejorative meaning in the popular consciousness of Tigray. Through a bitter linguistic play on words, Prosperity (ብልጽግና) has been recast as ብዕልግና (Biligina) in Tigrigna--a term associated with vulgarity, moral corruption, and misconduct. Consequently, Tigrayans who chose to align themselves with or join the PP came to be branded ባዕሊጉ (Baeligu), a charged label that, in this context, conveys profound condemnation of what is perceived as a betrayal of collective values, dignity, and solidarity. The post-Pretoria chapter was supposed to prove if the Prosperity Party had anything to offer Tigray--peace, justice, restoration, or rehabilitation. Instead, Tigray stood amidst ruin: over 600,000 killed, millions displaced , and its essential health, education, and transport infrastructure systematically looted and destroyed. Rather than repairing this damage , the regime has launched a new campaign to finish what it started and conquer the region completely. Ultimately, the ruling party has put nothing on Tigray's table except death or subjugation. The choice before Tigray is not simply between competing political arrangements ..." Across all phases of the war, Tigray's heritage--ancient and modern, sacred and secular--was targeted in a deliberate attempt to break a nation's spirit. From medieval monasteries to modern museums and historic icons, the assault aimed directly at what Tigrayans hold as their living soul. This physical destruction works hand-in-hand with historical abuse: through epistemic erasure, historiographical hegemony, and revisionist appropriation, ruling party figures seek to rewrite the legacy that their ethnic base belongs to the ancient legacy and history in Tigray. It is a dual-pronged strategy of cultural erasure and historical theft--destroying a people's living identity while co-opting their ancient legacy to legitimize the incumbent's party authority. Ultimately, the Prosperity Party's strategy is designed to weaken and depopulate substantive political entities like Tigray, replacing legitimate regional leadership with subservient proxies to entrench OPDO (currently, Oromo Prosperity Party) political and economic dominance. By attempting to project power into strategic maritime corridors like Assab, the ruling apparatus seeks to consolidate indefinite and irreversible rule--a centralized trajectory that is fundamentally incompatible with Tigray's historical identity and current struggle for self-determination. Self-Determination: Earned, learned, and craved Let us consider the words of Ms. Atsede Gebremedhin (a member of Tigray's 'Shig Weyane' (Revolutionary Torch) in the 1980s. She emphasized her message in Tigrigna, essentially conveying that although her generation envisioned Tigray's future within a federal framework, Ethiopian unity must never be traded for subjugation. When the choice is between self-determination and slavery, the pursuit of independence becomes unavoidable. Her words underscore a timeless principle: no political arrangement is worth sacrificing a people's freedom, dignity, and right to determine their own future. She further detailed her position, which can be, excerpted from the full speech, distilled into the following terms: "...regarding separation [from Ethiopia], we choose separation [independence]. Father Kidanu has been saying, 'We have separation as a second option.' We are putting it as an option, but if a progressive government is promulgated in Ethiopia, it [separation] will not be put as an option. It should not be taken that way. Only if a reactionary and slave system is to come to Ethiopia, we will have to separate ourselves to escape the slavery [oppression]. Therefore, separation is from the slavery and not from working-class people of Ethiopia." More than four decades later, Tigray has endured not only prolonged instability but also the devastating crime of genocide. Its longstanding adversaries, having regrouped after their defeat, returned with renewed force to inflict another wave of devastation marked by persecution, torture, genocide, and betrayal. These experiences have brought the question of self-determination back to the forefront of political consciousness. The aspiration for independence has increasingly gained prominence, finding expression through diverse political platforms, organized movements, public discourse, and cultural expression. Music, in particular, has become an important vehicle for expressing Tigrayan identity, historical consciousness, and national aspirations. Songs such as ዓዲ ኣላትኒ (I Have a Country), ሃ ገር እየ ዝደሊ (What I Want Is Independence), ትግራዋነት (The Essence of Being Tigrayan), ትግራይ ዓደይ (Tigray, My Nation), ትግራይ ኵሕሎ (Beautiful Tigray), ት ግራይ ምልባማ (Tigray, the Land of Wisdom), and many others reflect the growing significance of national identity, belonging, and aspirations for a sovereign future. This aspiration is neither new nor detached from history. It is rooted in generations of struggle and shaped by the historical experience of imperial nation-building and its devastating consequences for Tigray. It has been earned through sacrifice, strengthened by historical experience, and sustained by an enduring desire for freedom and a secured future. Yet, alongside this growing sense of national purpose, one fundamental question remains: How can this aspiration be translated into a viable, sustainable, and peaceful political future for Tigray? One step into a cruel destiny For the Prosperity government, war has served--and continues to serve--as an instrument for breaking the will, resistance, and collective determination of the people of Tigray. When the regime deploys starvation, foreign military forces, political coercion, and the co-optation of local elites to subdue an entire population, the struggle for self-determination ceases to be merely a political preference. It becomes an indispensable safeguard against subjugation and the permanent erosion of a people's freedom. A sober assessment of post-Pretoria reveals a deeply unsettling reality: Tigray appears to be entering the opening phase of a cruel political destiny--subjugation under the rule of the Prosperity government. As Tigray remains unliberated and increasingly subjected to the authority of the central regime, Ethiopia's overriding objective appears to be the dismantling of the political and institutional foundations that sustain Tigray's resistance and struggle for self-determination. Under the guise of pacification and political normalization, the federal government, helped by some Tigrayans who made their peace with the prime minister, appears to be pursuing a strategy of neutralizing resistance through the co-optation of Tigray's political and military elites. By offering administrative appointments, financial and material inducements, and assurances of personal survival, it seeks to hollow out the liberation struggle from within. Former defenders of Tigray's political aspirations risk becoming instruments and mouthpieces of the very central authority they once opposed. This political realignment risks a deeper ideological capitulation. A collective consciousness once anchored in freedom, dignity, and self-determination is gradually giving way to enforced subjugation and political assimilation. As former defenders align themselves with the very authority they once opposed, the moral and political foundations of the struggle erode, undermining its unifying force and leaving society increasingly disarmed--both politically and psychologically--and pressured to surrender long-term freedom for the precarious promise of immediate stability and survival. For those aligned with Abiy Ahmed's government, life under external control appears increasingly acceptable and normal. For those who continue to resist, however, subjugation remains unacceptable at any cost. Meanwhile, the central regime and its local partners increasingly portray the historical struggle led by the TPLF as outdated, destructive, or an obstacle to "peace and development." As these narratives take hold, submission risks being recast as political pragmatism, while historical memory and collective political consciousness are distorted or erased. Future generations may consequently be led to view the sacrifices of their predecessors and the TPLF's struggle not as acts of resistance and defense of the right to self-rule but as misguided and costly mistakes. Coercive assimilation, state-led social engineering What is presented as integration may, under occupation and political subordination, become a state-engineered project of assimilation. By extending central government institutions and security structures into Tigray's social and political life, the state could displace local authority, dismantle sovereign institutions, and erode the foundations of self-governance. Prolonged military occupation could thus serve not merely to administer territory but to impose a far-reaching political and social transformation. This process could entail the imposition of political, cultural, and administrative arrangements through military coercion, legislative control, divide-and-rule tactics, and the systematic suppression of local autonomy. Rather than recognize Tigray's distinct historical experience and political aspirations, the central state could seek to remake its institutions and public life in its own image and in accordance with its political priorities. The danger extends beyond institutional control to demographic and territorial engineering. In the aftermath of mass atrocities, such developments raise grave concerns about whether political domination could evolve into a broader project of demographic transformation, threatening the long-term continuity of the Tigray people. As this trajectory becomes entrenched, many Tigrayans--particularly those unwilling to abandon the pursuit of self-determination--may come to see leaving their homeland as the only remaining means of resisting subjugation. Those who remain, meanwhile, could find themselves trapped in a deeply fractured society, divided between accommodation and resistance, privilege and deprivation, and outward compliance and inward resentment. Tigray risks becoming a society of happy slaves and unhappy slaves--one in which subjugation is normalized for some and silently endured by others. This division between those aligned with the central government and those resisting subjugation could harden into an entrenched system of divide and rule. By cultivating competing loyalties and interests within Tigrayan society, the regime could fracture collective solidarity, weaken organized resistance, and obstruct a unified political response. The result could be an "enemy within" syndrome, in which internal suspicion becomes a major obstacle to future unity. Mutual distrust could gradually replace the quiet solidarity, shared understanding, and knowing glances through which Tigrayans sustained one another during the darkest years of siege and blockade. A society once united by shared suffering and resistance could become consumed by suspicion over who has accommodated the system, who has resisted it, and who can still be trusted. Indefinite social discord The existing horizontal divisions within Tigrayan elites--expressed through political realignments, competing strategic visions, and conflicting interpretations of the postwar order--risk hardening into a prolonged and intergenerational rupture. If centralizing and assimilationist policies become entrenched, Tigray could face not only a political struggle over its future but also an internal war over its history, identity, and collective memory. Self-determination must once again become the organizing principle of Tigray's political future." One generation may grow increasingly exposed to central government-sponsored narratives, while another remains committed to preserving Tigray's historical struggle for self-rule rights, convictions, and aspirations. Such a rupture would not remain confined to political organizations or public institutions. It could penetrate the most intimate structures of the society. The long-term damage would extend far beyond political disagreement, undermining the social trust upon which collective life depends. The collapse of social contract of sacrifice Perhaps one of the most devastating long-term consequences of an unaddressed political defeat and perceived internal betrayal would be the destruction of society's capacity for collective mobilization. When the social contract of sacrifice is broken, a profound cynicism may take hold toward political leadership, military institutions, and the very causes for which ordinary people were once prepared to make extraordinary sacrifices. For a population to endure the horrors of war, there must be a fundamental, often unspoken covenant among the people, their fighters, their leadership, and the cause they serve. That covenant rests on a shared understanding: sacrifice must have meaning; those who fall must be remembered and honored; the suffering of the population must not be exploited; and leaders must not trade away the collective cause for their personal security or political survival. When this covenant is violated, the consequences can endure for generations. The public may lose confidence in those who call for sacrifice, and future appeals for mobilization may be met with profound skepticism. People may no longer regard military mobilization as an honorable defense of their homeland and collective aspirations but as a political instrument through which ordinary citizens bear the ultimate costs while political and military elites negotiate their own survival and interests. The memory of betrayal can therefore become a powerful deterrent to future collective action. Even when an existential threat emerges, a population that has lost confidence in its leadership may hesitate to mobilize, fearing that its sacrifices will once again be squandered or betrayed. The f
ethiopia.summary: Tigray's complex relationship with Ethiopia is marked by historical oppression and betrayal, juxtaposed with moments of significant political influence. The era of Meles Zenawi initially brought hope to Tigrayans, who believed in a shared identity based on self-determination and equality. However, this trust has been shattered, revealing a deep sense of betrayal as the Ethiopian state has failed to protect Tigray's autonomy and rights. The 2020-2022 war exemplified this betrayal, leading to immense loss of life and destruction of infrastructure. The Prosperity Party's ideology has further marginalized Tigray, fostering resentment and a desire for self-determination among its people. Cultural erasure and historical appropriation have compounded these grievances, as Tigrayans seek to reclaim their identity and future. Amidst ongoing violence and geopolitical manipulation, the aspiration for independence has gained momentum, reflecting a historical struggle for dignity and sovereignty. The question remains: how can Tigray's aspirations for self-determination translate into a sustainable political future? (159 words)

ethiopia.content: Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace Ayin Network TPLF fighters (file photo). 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — US Republican Representative Jim Baird has proposed two pieces of legislation seeking to link expanded trade and economic cooperation with Ethiopia and Eritrea to progress toward lasting peace, as tensions between the neighboring countries continue to raise fears of a renewed interstate conflict. The proposed Ethiopia SPARK Act and Eritrea PILLAR Act would use US agricultural exports, farm equipment, technical expertise and cooperation in critical minerals development as economic incentives for both countries to pursue peace, according to a report by The Hill published on November 19. The legislation, shared exclusively in draft form with The Hill , also seeks to strengthen US economic influence in the Horn of Africa and reduce China's foothold in the region. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Under the proposed measures, Ethiopia and Eritrea would be offered opportunities for formal trade negotiations and expanded access to US agricultural products, including corn, soybeans, soybean meal and livestock feed, as well as farm machinery, agricultural research and technical assistance, contingent on steps toward establishing lasting peace. The proposals also envisage US assistance in developing the region's mineral resources, including gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron ore, potash, cement, limestone, natural gas and oil, alongside cooperation on port infrastructure. Washington could offer reduced tariffs and improved trade terms as additional incentives. Baird, a Republican from Indiana and member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa, described the initiative as an opportunity to build economic partnerships with African countries while limiting the influence of US adversaries. "African nations are primed for partnership," Baird said in a statement to The Hill . "The continent is rich in natural resources and home to a young, growing population eager for greater economic opportunity. In Indiana and across America's heartland, we have the agricultural expertise and technological know-how to help unlock that potential and build lasting economic partnerships." "East Africa has tremendous potential, with the benefit of limited influence from America's adversaries, like China," he added. Baird said the proposed economic cooperation could provide a foundation for regional stability and prosperity, arguing that African countries pursuing peaceful cooperation and economic growth would find a willing partner in the United States. The initiative comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with competing claims over sovereign Red Sea access, mutual accusations of interference and reported military buildups along their shared border heightening fears of a wider confrontation. The deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries broke down on October 1, following Ethiopia's closure of its embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats, a move reciprocated by Eritrea . Both governments have subsequently exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, while reports of troop movements, drone strikes and artillery activity around the disputed border town of Badme have intensified concerns about a possible military escalation. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Nearly 700,000 Displaced By Moyale Conflict in Southern Ethiopia: Islamic Relief - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Nearly 700,000 Displaced By Moyale Conflict in Southern Ethiopia: Islamic Relief 19 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Nearly 700,000 people have been displaced by Moyale conflict along Ethiopia's border with Kenya and Somalia, with widespread destruction of homes and disruption of essential services, Islamic Relief Ethiopia said, warning of a deepening humanitarian crisis. In a statement, the humanitarian organization estimated that 329,000 people had been displaced from Dawa Zone in the Somali Region and another 359,798 across southern Oromia, bringing the total to approximately 688,800. The fighting, which Islamic Relief said began on October 22 between Somali and Oromo communities, has reportedly spread as far as 300 kilometers from the border town of Moyale. The latest figures mark a significant escalation of the crisis that began in Moyale on October 18, amid renewed territorial tensions between Oromia and Somali regional forces . The violence has since spread into surrounding districts in Borana Zone, with mediation efforts involving local elders and federal intervention failing to secure a lasting cessation of hostilities. Fighting reportedly resumed on November 16, causing further destruction of homes and businesses, according to Addis Standard's recent in-depth reporting . Islamic Relief said the conflict had destroyed homes, businesses and fuel stations, while severely disrupting health, nutrition, water and sanitation services. Civilians remain vulnerable to attacks, and hundreds of thousands of displaced people will require assistance before they can safely return home. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The crisis has also spilled across the border into Kenya, where approximately 50,000 people have reportedly sought safety and humanitarian assistance, placing additional pressure on local services and host communities. "This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia," said Kedir Musema Hameza, head of programs at Islamic Relief Ethiopia. "Unfortunately, when conflict like this arises it is vulnerable civilians that end up paying a high price. We are seeing that now with this mass displacement of nearly 700,000 people fleeing the violence. This is a serious humanitarian incident which we are working to respond to," he added. Hameza said the organization had received reports from local sources that fighting had subsided and that UN teams were travelling to affected areas to assess the condition of displaced communities and the extent of the destruction. "Homes have been burnt and peoples lives have been hit. We need funding to respond and help these suffering communities," he said. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, India Seek to Deepen Strategic Trade and Investment Partnership - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia, India Seek to Deepen Strategic Trade and Investment Partnership 19 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia and India have discussed about expanding bilateral trade and investment cooperation, with Ethiopia highlighting opportunities created by its ongoing economic reforms and access to the wider African market. The discussions took place when Minister of Trade and Regional Integration, Yasmin Wohabrebbi, received India's newly appointed Ambassador to Ethiopia, Devesh Uttam, at her office, where they exchanged views on bilateral trade, investment, addressing trade imbalances and regional market integration. During the meeting, the Minister underscored that Ethiopia-India relations are built on longstanding diplomatic ties, mutual respect, South-South cooperation and friendship between the two countries' leaders, the ministry shared on its social media page. She also commended India's continued support for Ethiopia's efforts to join the World Trade Organization (WTO), particularly its backing throughout the various rounds of accession negotiations. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Highlighting the opportunities emerging from Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform, Yasmin said the ongoing reforms are gradually opening up the economy and expanding private sector participation. She pointed to progress in opening selected sectors to domestic and foreign investors, reforming the financial sector to facilitate the entry of foreign banks, improving access to foreign exchange and streamlining tax, customs and trade licensing procedures through digitization. The Minister further said Ethiopia's membership in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) offers Indian companies opportunity to establish investment and manufacturing operations in the country, access the wider African market and develop regional value chains. For his part, Ambassador Devesh Uttam reaffirmed India's commitment to strengthening relations with Ethiopia, describing the country as an important partner for India and a gateway to the wider African market. He noted that bilateral relations have developed into a strategic partnership, citing the outcomes of recent high-level visits by leaders and foreign ministers of the two countries. A Government of Political Theatre, Misleading Statements, and Weak Leadership Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Abdiaziz Hassan Giyaajo Amalo Friday November 20, 2026\ Somalia deserves a Prime Minister who understands the responsibilities of his office, exercises independent leadership, and communicates honestly with the Somali people. Unfortunately, the current political environment raises serious questions about the effectiveness, authority, and credibility of the Prime Minister. His public statements concerning the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) illustrate the growing problem of political communication in Mogadishu: taking credit for international decisions, confusing separate United Nations mandates, and presenting developments beyond the government’s control as achievements of the federal administration. The Prime Minister should explain precisely what his government has accomplished regarding UNSOS. Did the Federal Government formally cancel the mission, or did an existing United Nations mandate reach its scheduled expiration date? These are fundamentally different matters, and the Somali public deserves an honest explanation. UNSOS Is Not the Same as UNTMIS There is an important distinction that the Prime Minister should understand before making public declarations. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) officially concluded its operations on October 31, 2026, following a two-year transition requested by the Somali government. UNSOS, however, is a separate United Nations operation responsible for providing essential logistical support to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and participating Somali security forces. According to the United Nations, UNSOS’s existing authorization for 2026 remains in place, with the current AUSSOM authorization scheduled to expire on December 31, 2026. Furthermore, discussions about the future of UNSOS involve international funding decisions, particularly the position of the United States, one of its major financial supporters. Therefore, claiming that the Somali government independently cancelled UNSOS would require documentary evidence and clarification from the United Nations Security Council. An Empty Suit at the Top of Government The deeper problem is not simply one statement about the United Nations. It is the apparent absence of strong, independent executive leadership. A Prime Minister should not function as a ceremonial spokesperson whose principal responsibility is to defend presidential decisions or announce political victories that have not been achieved. Somalia needs a Prime Minister who can challenge bad policies, demand accountability, coordinate national institutions, and represent the interests of the entire country. A government cannot build public confidence through political publicity while the country continues to experience insecurity, constitutional disagreements, institutional weaknesses, and economic hardship. The Prime Minister must demonstrate that his office has genuine authority and is not merely an extension of Villa Somalia. Somalia Needs Leadership, Not Political Public Relations At a time when Somalia faces serious political and security challenges, the country cannot afford leadership built around exaggerated announcements and misleading political narratives. The Prime Minister should answer several important questions: 1. Did the Federal Government officially request the cancellation of UNSOS? 2. Is there a formal United Nations Security Council decision terminating UNSOS? 3. Why is the government presenting the conclusion of UNTMIS as though it were the cancellation of UNSOS? 4. What alternative logistical arrangements will support AUSSOM and Somali security forces if international assistance is reduced? 5. What independent authority does the Prime Minister exercise in making national policy? These are legitimate questions of public accountability, not personal attacks. Conclusion: Somalia Deserves a Real Prime Minister Somalia does not need an empty suit occupying the office of Prime Minister. It needs a serious statesman capable of exercising constitutional authority, defending national interests, and telling the Somali people the truth. Leadership is not measured by press conferences, political slogans, or the ability to take credit for decisions made by international institutions. It is measured by results, integrity, accountability, and the ability to govern. If the Prime Minister cannot distinguish between the expiration of one United Nations mission and the continuing mandate of another, the public has every reason to demand a clearer explanation. Somalia needs leadership, not political theatre. The office of Prime Minister must represent national responsibility, not merely serve as a political decoration inside Villa Somalia. Important factual distinction: UNTMIS closed on October 31, 2026. UNSOS is separate, and its current 2026 authorization has not yet expired as of November 19, 2026. The distinction is documented by the United Nations UNSOS mandate⁠. In a statement issued Thursday, Nov. 19, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs criticized what it described as escalating hostility from Mogadishu, saying Somalia's actions were undermining longstanding cooperation between the two countries. advertisements “The United Arab Emirates strongly denounced the escalatory and hostile approach by the Somali government toward the UAE,” the ministry said, describing Somalia's position as irresponsible and damaging to bilateral relations. The statement came hours after Somalia's Cabinet ordered the Emirati ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its own ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations. The Somali government said the measures were intended to protect its sovereignty and territorial integrity following allegations that the UAE had interfered in its internal political and security affairs. Responding to the diplomatic measures, the UAE Foreign Ministry said relations between countries should be based on mutual interests rather than domestic political disagreements. The ministry accused Somalia's government of allowing internal power struggles to affect bilateral relations, warning that the consequences could harm the interests of both populations. The UAE also disclosed that it had closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomatic personnel in January 2026, citing what it described as hostile actions by Somali authorities. According to the ministry, the decision followed disagreements over Somalia's cancellation of bilateral agreements involving the two countries. The disclosure raises questions about the practical implications of Somalia's latest expulsion order, given Abu Dhabi's assertion that it had already withdrawn its diplomatic staff from Mogadishu earlier this year. The ministry did not clarify whether any Emirati diplomatic personnel had subsequently returned to Somalia or whether its ambassador was physically present in Mogadishu when the expulsion order was issued. The latest exchange follows accusations by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud that the UAE has provided financial, political and security assistance to regional administrations and armed groups operating outside federal government control. In a televised address Tuesday, Hassan Sheikh accused Abu Dhabi of undermining Somalia's national unity through its relationships with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland. He also criticized Emirati involvement in the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, arguing that agreements involving strategic national assets should be negotiated through Somalia's federal government. The UAE has rejected accusations that its policies are intended to undermine Somalia's stability. On Wednesday, Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, accused Hassan Sheikh of prioritizing personal political considerations over Somalia's national interests. Gargash defended the UAE's longstanding relationship with Somalia and warned against allowing domestic political rivalries to escalate into regional disputes. Despite the diplomatic confrontation, the UAE Foreign Ministry emphasized that its disagreements with the Somali government did not extend to the Somali people. It reaffirmed its appreciation for the longstanding relationship between the two populations, particularly the Somali community living in the UAE and Somalis visiting the Gulf country. “The UAE remains committed to preserving and strengthening these ties and shared interests,” the ministry said. Somalia and the UAE have maintained diplomatic, commercial and security relations for decades, but disagreements over regional port agreements, security cooperation and relations with Somali federal member states have increasingly strained ties. The dispute intensified in January when Somalia's Cabinet annulled agreements with the UAE covering defense, security and economic cooperation. Thursday's statements mark a further deterioration in relations, with both governments accusing the other of undermining cooperation while maintaining that their disagreements are with government policies rather than the people of either country. PHOTO/@DrWorkneh/X Somalia and Kenya have welcomed the entry into force of the 2023 Treaty Establishing the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), marking a new phase in efforts to strengthen regional cooperation in the Greater Horn of Africa. The treaty took effect on November 16, 2026, following its ratification by Somalia in January, which provided the final threshold required for its implementation. advertisements In separate statements issued on Wednesday, November 18, the two countries congratulated IGAD member states and the organisation’s Secretariat, describing the development as an important step towards strengthening the institution’s legal and operational framework. Somalia, a founding member of IGAD, said the development coincides with 40 years of regional cooperation since the establishment of the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development (IGADD) in 1986. “The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of the Federal Republic of Somalia welcomes the entry into force of the 2023 Treaty Establishing the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) on 16 November 2026, and congratulates IGAD Member States and the IGAD Secretariat on this milestone,” read the notice in part. Somalia reaffirms commitment to regional cooperation In a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mogadishu said the new treaty strengthens the legal and institutional foundation of IGAD and reinforces the commitment of member states to peace, security, economic integration and sustainable development. The ministry reaffirmed Somalia’s commitment to the principles of sovereignty, territorial integrity, mutual respect and regional solidarity. It also expressed readiness to work with other member states to ensure the full implementation of the treaty and strengthen cooperation across the region. Somalia further commended the IGAD Secretariat, under the leadership of Executive Secretary Dr Workneh Gebeyehu, for advancing the organisation’s mandate. The ministry said it remained committed to building a stronger, more effective and united IGAD that serves the interests of people across the Greater Horn of Africa. Kenya backs stronger IGAD framework Kenya’s Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs also congratulated the regional organisation, noting that the 2023 treaty succeeds the 1996 Agreement Establishing IGAD. Nairobi said the organisation had evolved significantly from its original focus on combating drought and desertification to embrace a wider regional development agenda. Its current mandate includes promoting trade and free movement, infrastructure development, innovation, climate resilience, peace and security. Kenya said the treaty comes into force at a challenging time for the region, which continues to face political, security, economic and climate-related vulnerabilities despite its considerable natural resources, human potential and strategic geographical position. The ministry expressed confidence that the new legal framework would transform IGAD into a rules-based institution capable of advancing regional prosperity and addressing longstanding challenges. Kenya also paid tribute to member states for their continued commitment to the organisation and commended the Secretariat and its staff, led by Gebeyehu, for their work. IGAD marks 40 years of regional cooperation The entry into force of the treaty comes as IGAD marks four decades since its establishment in 1986. The organisation was initially formed as IGADD to coordinate efforts among countries in the region to address drought and desertification. It was later transformed into IGAD in 1996, expanding its mandate to cover wider areas of regional development, economic cooperation and security. The 2023 treaty seeks to provide a stronger legal basis for the organisation to coordinate these responsibilities and improve cooperation among its member states. Both Somalia and Kenya have reaffirmed their commitment to working through IGAD to advance regional peace, security and economic integration. The two countries also expressed support for the organisation’s efforts to strengthen cooperation among member states as the Greater Horn of Africa confronts persistent political, economic and environmental challenges. The treaty’s entry into force marks a significant institutional development for the bloc as it seeks to deepen regional integration and strengthen its capacity to respond to shared challenges. SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Mogadishu (Somalia Today) — Somalia on Thursday gave the United Arab Emirates’ ambassador 72 hours to leave the country and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi for consultations, accusing the Gulf state of “blatant aggression” against its sovereignty. The cabinet directed the foreign ministry to put Somalia’s case to other governments and international organisations. The UAE foreign ministry denounced what it called Mogadishu’s “escalatory and hostile approach”. It said the UAE had closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomats in January, blaming the Somali government’s treatment of the mission and its cancellation of bilateral agreements. The dispute has centred on who can sign port and security deals with Abu Dhabi. Mogadishu says that authority rests with the federal government, while Somaliland and several regional administrations maintain they can strike their own agreements. Here is how ties between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi unravelled over more than a decade: Ports and military ties, 2014–2017 The UAE began training Somali troops in 2014, the year it reopened its diplomatic mission in Mogadishu. The programme was part of an international effort to build up Somalia’s army as it fought Al-Shabaab alongside African Union forces. Abu Dhabi later said it had built three training centres and paid the salaries of 2,407 Somali soldiers. It also said it had helped run Puntland’s maritime police force to combat piracy. The UAE was working with authorities that controlled their own ports and security forces as well as with the federal government. In 2016, Somaliland awarded Dubai-based DP World a 30-year concession to run and develop Berbera on the Gulf of Aden. The company announced plans to invest up to $442 million. The port offered landlocked Ethiopia another route to the sea and gave Somaliland a major commercial agreement with a Gulf partner. Somaliland had governed itself since declaring independence in 1991. Mogadishu regarded it as part of Somalia and said agreements over the port required federal approval. In February 2017, Somaliland’s parliament approved separate plans for an Emirati military base at Berbera. The UAE was then part of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, across the Gulf of Aden. Two months later, P&O Ports, owned by the Dubai government, signed a 30-year concession with Puntland to manage and expand Bosaso. The company put the proposed investment at $336 million. Puntland’s parliament approved the deal in July. Somalia’s ports minister, Mariam Aweis, told UN monitors that seaports were national assets and that the federal government had to approve port concessions. The monitors warned that disputes over control of ports and their revenues could undermine stability. Gulf rift and cash seizure, 2017–2018 Those disputes over regional autonomy hardened into an open diplomatic crisis in June 2017, when Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt cut ties with Qatar, accusing it of backing terrorism. Qatar denied the charge. The government of Somali President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed, known as Farmaajo, declared itself neutral. Puntland, Galmudug and Hirshabelle issued statements siding with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. In September, the federal government rebuked the regional administrations and said foreign policy was its responsibility. Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire’s office reiterated the position the cabinet had taken in June. The dispute over Berbera sharpened in March 2018, when DP World signed a deal with Somaliland and Ethiopia under which Addis Ababa was to take a 19 per cent stake in the port. On 12 March, Somalia’s lower house voted to bar DP World and rejected the port agreements. On 8 April, Somali authorities seized $9.6 million in cash from an Emirati aircraft at Mogadishu airport. Somali security officials told Voice of America they considered the money illegal and suspected it was meant to undermine security. “It’s for the salary of the Somali soldiers,” the UAE’s ambassador told VOA, saying the money was for Somalia’s defence ministry. Abu Dhabi condemned the seizure and said the payment fell under its military cooperation agreement with Somalia. On 11 April, Mogadishu said it would take over the training and payment of soldiers in the programme. Days later, Abu Dhabi cited the seizure as it announced it was ending the training mission. The UAE also closed a military facility and the Sheikh Zayed Hospital in Mogadishu. The cash remained in Somalia’s central bank for four years. A diplomatic reset, 2022–2024 Relations remained frozen for nearly four years until January 2022, when Prime Minister Mohamed Hussein Roble publicly apologised for the seizure as he welcomed a shipment of Emirati drought aid at Mogadishu airport. He pledged to return the money and said his government wanted closer ties with the UAE. Somalia returned the $9.6 million in May, days after lawmakers elected Hassan Sheikh Mohamud to replace Farmaajo. Later that month, Mohamud thanked the UAE for its response to the drought when he received the Emirati ambassador at the presidential palace. On 22 June, Mohamud met UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi. The Emirati leader reaffirmed his country’s support for Somalia’s stability and development. Mohamud said he wanted to expand cooperation and help improve security in the region. On 6 February 2023, Somalia’s cabinet approved a military and security agreement with the UAE that also covered counter-terrorism, according to a briefing to the UN Security Council. Somalia was seeking to expand its armed forces and take over security responsibilities from the African Union mission. In March 2023, DP World and Somaliland opened the Berbera Economic Zone on the road to Ethiopia. The port had added a container terminal in 2021. Somaliland had continued working with the Emirati company through years of strained ties between Abu Dhabi and Mogadishu. In February 2024, Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for an attack on the General Gordon base in Mogadishu that killed four Emirati service members and a Bahraini officer. They were there to train Somali forces. Israel’s recognition, 2025–2026 The rebuilt partnership held until late 2025, when a diplomatic breakthrough by Hargeisa upended regional alignments. On 26 December 2025, Israel became the first country to recognise Somaliland as an independent state since its 1991 declaration, signing a mutual recognition pact with Hargeisa. Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi said his administration would join the Abraham Accords, under which Israel had normalised ties with the UAE and other Arab countries in 2020. The former British protectorate had united with Italian Somaliland in 1960 to form Somalia before declaring independence in 1991 as civil war engulfed the country. No UN member state had recognised its claim for more than three decades. Mogadishu condemned Israel’s decision as a “deliberate attack” on its sovereignty. The African Union Commission rejected the recognition and reaffirmed its support for Somalia’s territorial integrity. Arab and Islamic states issued statements denouncing the move, though Somali officials later pointed out that Abu Dhabi had declined to sign on to the condemnations, deepening suspicion in Mogadishu over the UAE’s role. On 6 January 2026, the UAE and the African Union Commission issued a joint statement after talks in Addis Ababa reaffirming their support for Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability. Yemen dispute, January 2026 Days after Abu Dhabi reaffirmed its support for Somalia’s territorial integrity in Addis Ababa, a separate crisis across the Gulf of Aden pulled Mogadishu into a confrontation between its Gulf partners. Saudi Arabia and the UAE had fought together against the Houthis in Yemen before backing rival Yemeni forces. Abu Dhabi supported the Southern Transitional Council, whose separatist forces had advanced through southern Yemen in December 2025. The Saudi-led coalition accused the UAE on 8 January 2026 of helping the council’s leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, escape from Yemen after he missed crisis talks in Riyadh. The coalition said al-Zubaidi travelled by sea from Yemen to Berbera in Somaliland and onward to Mogadishu under the supervision of Emirati officers, before the aircraft flew to a military airport in Abu Dhabi. The coalition’s statement named the UAE officer involved, though its account left it unclear whether he was still aboard on the final leg. The council also said al-Zubaidi had been asked to travel to Saudi Arabia under threat. Reuters reported no immediate comment from the UAE or the council on the coalition’s account. Somalia’s Immigration and Citizenship Agency said it had opened an investigation into whether its airports had been used to move al-Zubaidi without authorisation. It said that would amount to a serious breach of national sovereignty if confirmed. The incident placed Mogadishu directly in the middle of the widening rivalry between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Mogadishu annuls deals, January–May 2026 Mogadishu moved swiftly to curb Emirati access. On 9 January, Somalia Today reported, citing sources, that federal authorities had barred Emirati military and cargo flights after an alleged breach of Somali airspace. The sources said the restrictions spared commercial airlines. Three days later, Somalia’s cabinet annulled all agreements with the UAE, including those on ports, government institutions, defence and security. The foreign ministry said the decision covered arrangements in Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo and cooperation involving federal institutions and member states. The cabinet cited threats to Somalia’s sovereignty, independence and unity. Government sources told Somalia Today at the time that Israel’s recognition of Somaliland had prompted the decision. The foreign ministry said it would notify Abu Dhabi and brief regional and international partners. It said future cooperation would have to respect Somalia’s sovereignty, its constitution and international law. Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland challenged Mogadishu’s authority to end their agreements with Abu Dhabi. Puntland said it would maintain its ties with the UAE, including the Bosaso concession. Jubbaland called the decision “null and void” and said it would keep its security and development agreements. “The UAE is here to stay,” said Somaliland’s minister of the presidency, Khadar Hussein Abdi. DP World continued to operate Berbera. Somalia Today reported on 12 January, citing witnesses and officials, that the UAE had begun moving personnel and equipment out of positions in Somalia as Mogadishu cancelled the agreements. On 4 May, Somalia’s foreign ministry denied reports that Mogadishu had expelled the Emirati ambassador and said the UAE’s mission was fully operational. It urged the media and the public to rely on official announcements. Diplomatic rupture, October–November 2026 Despite that denial, underlying tensions over Somaliland and regional security deals resurfaced in the autumn. Speaking to Al Jazeera in October, Mohamud accused Abu Dhabi of increasingly siding with Somaliland and encouraging its bid to break away. In a televised address on 17 November, Mohamud accused the UAE of bypassing the federal government in port deals and helping set up bases and armed units outside Somalia’s chain of command. He said Abu Dhabi had given political and financial backing to regional administrations at odds with Mogadishu. Mohamud also accused the UAE of playing a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland and said it had declined to sign Arab and Islamic statements condemning the move. He alleged that Abu Dhabi had used Berbera in January to move a Yemeni separatist leader without federal consent. The next day, Somalia’s foreign ministry said foreign governments must deal through federal institutions and pledged to take lawful measures to defend the country’s sovereignty. Anwar Gargash, the UAE president’s diplomatic adviser, questioned whether Mohamud was putting his own interests ahead of Somalia’s. He said the UAE had stood by Somalia and its people “in their darkest hours” and blamed domestic power struggles for drawing the country into regional rivalries. “Pack your bags and leave,” Defence Minister Ahmed Moalim Fiqi told the Emirati ambassador in a post on X after Thursday’s decision. While Abu Dhabi’s statement did not directly address the expulsion deadline, Somalia Today confirmed that Ambassador Ahmed Jumaa Alremeithi remained working in Mogadishu on Thursday, though the mission’s staff had been scaled back months earlier. Reuters reported on Thursday that the UAE was still paying salaries and providing logistical support for about 3,400 Somali military police and special forces personnel in and around Mogadishu. somalia.summary: Somalia's diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have deteriorated significantly over the past decade, culminating in the recent expulsion of the UAE ambassador from Somalia. The Somali government accused the UAE of "blatant aggression" against its sovereignty, prompting a reciprocal withdrawal of its envoy from Abu Dhabi. Tensions escalated following disputes over port and security agreements, particularly as regional administrations like Somaliland pursued independent deals with the UAE, which Mogadishu deemed unconstitutional. The situation worsened in 2018 when Somalia seized $9.6 million from an Emirati aircraft, leading to the UAE halting military training programs. Although relations briefly improved after a public apology from Somalia in 2022, they soured again after Israel recognized Somaliland as independent in late 2025, a move Somalia condemned. The ongoing rivalry between Saudi Arabia and the UAE further complicates Somalia's position, as recent incidents have raised concerns about violations of its sovereignty.

(AFP) The United Arab Emirates strongly condemned on Thursday the “escalatory and hostile approach” adopted by the Somali government toward the UAE. The approach “reflects irresponsible positions that undermine bilateral relations and weaken the foundations of cooperation between the two countries,” said a statement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It stressed that decisions affecting relations between countries “should be guided by shared interests and should remain free of political considerations and internal conflicts.” Somalia on Thursday expelled the UAE ambassador, accusing the Gulf nation of interfering in its internal affairs. The Ministry expressed regret over the Somali government’s “attempts to bring its internal power struggles into bilateral relations in a manner which could adversely affect the interests of the two brotherly peoples.” The Ministry noted that “the UAE had previously closed its embassy in the Somali capital, Mogadishu, and withdrawn its diplomatic staff in January 2026, citing hostile practices by the Somali government toward the UAE’s embassy and policies, including its decisions to cancel bilateral agreements concluded between the two countries.” The Ministry underscored “the UAE’s deep appreciation for the brotherly Somali people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples, particularly with the Somali community residing in the UAE and Somali visitors.” The UAE remains committed to preserving and strengthening these ties and shared interests, it stressed.
